deep_why: The core challenge is mapping abstract campaign language to concrete product types without direct labels. The method works because large language models trained on broad text can infer intent from marketing language by capturing semantic relationships humans also recognize. When the model then retrieves candidate product types from a taxonomy using these inferred intents, it narrows the ambiguous space into specific, verifiable categories. Relevance scoring by structured rules further filters false matches. The key insight is that campaign intent and product affinity cohere: campaigns that discuss certain themes will attract users seeking related product categories, so labeling user purchases matching the inferred types creates training signal aligned with causality. This lets the ranking model learn from synthetic but semantically honest supervision.

The problem is designing agent collaboration graphs that generalize across unrelated tasks, yet most methods train one model per task and fail on new domains. This approach works because a mixture-of-experts architecture can learn to recognize structural patterns that repeat across diverse collaboration problems: certain task types naturally call for hierarchical routing, others need peer-to-peer sharing. By pre-training on many canonical topologies and then specializing via gating, the model learns which sub-networks activate for which structural signatures. A task-aware encoder filters only relevant node properties, reducing noise. The reason this generalizes is that abstract collaboration patterns (star topologies for centralized decisions, mesh topologies for consensus) solve fundamental coordination tradeoffs regardless of domain. Fine-tuning on validated real graphs ensures the selected patterns actually work.

Federated clustering fails when clients disagree on the number of clusters because naive averaging produces prototypes that belong to nobody's intended semantic granularity. The solution separates each client's data into what it shares (public patterns) and what it keeps private (domain-specific noise), then aggregates only the public parts by measuring similarity between reconstructed cluster-level graphs. This works because public patterns are the stable, repeatable structures that persist across clients—the semantic common ground—while private patterns are local idiosyncrasies that would corrupt averaging. By aligning clusters through affinities (how similar their public representations are), not by forcing cluster counts to match, the method lets clients with different granularities cooperate honestly. Privacy follows naturally: only summary statistics of public information leave each client.

Finding rumor sources from partial observations in social graphs is hard because many different source locations can explain the same infection pattern, yet deep learning approaches explode in parameters by stacking auxiliary features. This method works because source localization is fundamentally a ranking problem over candidate nodes: nodes closer to the observed infected region are more likely sources. Pre-training on synthetic cascades with known sources teaches the model to recognize which structural positions tend to propagate observed patterns. Prompt learning then reuses this pre-trained ranker without retraining, treating new queries as in-context tasks. The key is that source-induced diffusion has regular statistical properties—closer sources infect faster—so a model trained on one synthetic distribution generalizes to different cascades quickly. Keeping the base model small and adapting only the prompt avoids parameter explosion and enables real-time deployment.

Time series across multiple sites have both common patterns everyone shares and local quirks unique to each client, yet federated learning struggles when these vary site-to-site. The method separates common structure (low-frequency oscillations that repeat across all domains) from personalized detail (high-frequency noise specific to each location) by routing them through different paths in the model. Low-frequency components stay synchronized across clients when averaged, while high-frequency residuals learn locally. This works because real time signals decompose into smooth trends plus local deviations: the trend carries shared information worth pooling, but deviations reflect site-specific conditions that shouldn't be averaged. A frequency-aware loss enforces this split so the global and local modules don't compete. Gated fusion then reweights these components adaptively per prediction, letting each location trust the shared trend or its own history as conditions warrant.

Recommendation graphs have wildly different local structures—some dense hubs, some sparse branches—yet standard methods assume uniform geometry and propagate information on a flat space. This work reframes learning as a physical process unfolding on a curved manifold where distances stretch and shrink to match topology: near dense regions distances compress (interactions cluster tightly), in sparse areas they expand (information spreads farther). The metric tensor (a learnable per-node distance measure) bends space to align with actual local topology. Information then flows naturally along geodesics (shortest paths on this curved surface) without needing tangent-space tricks. Why this works: real interaction graphs contain hierarchical structure—communities are tightly knit, inter-community links are bridges—and curved spaces natively represent this. Propagation along geodesics preserves these distinctions, so distant but structurally important nodes remain reachable.

Pathology anomalies are subtle local defects invisible to global vision models trained on natural images, and text prompts alone can't describe what hasn't been seen. The method works by enforcing a bidirectional alignment: visual features from the region of interest first ground text prompts in actual pixel evidence (so 'abnormal mitochondria' becomes tethered to what's really there), then refined prompts guide the visual encoder to spotlight those same anomalies in feedback loops. This two-way grounding works because language and vision encode complementary signals: vision captures exact shapes and textures, language organizes semantic categories. By forcing them to constrain each other, each modality overcomes its weakness. Few-shot settings benefit because even one labeled anomaly can teach the visual encoder what 'abnormal' means for this specific tissue, and semantic prompts articulate domain knowledge that fills gaps. Geometric prototypes add robustness by giving fallback decisions when semantic confidence is low.

Teaching language models to handle graphs faces a fundamental problem: just encoding graphs into sequences and supervising with text leaves the language model dominant, barely using graph structure. The method addresses this by adding explicit graph reconstruction: the model not only predicts text tokens aligned with the input graph, but also reconstructs the graph itself from those tokens. This works because reconstruction is a stronger constraint—it forces the model to preserve graph information end-to-end. Information theory guarantees that maximizing the mutual information between input graphs and learned representations lets both graph and text supervision pull in aligned directions. Reconstruction adds graph supervision directly, improving this upper bound on alignment. The model learns token sequences that capture both semantic meaning (text alignment) and structural correctness (graph reconstruction), preventing the text signal from drowning out graph signal.

In document review workflows, knowing when to stop requires estimating true recall without examining every document—prohibitively expensive at low prevalence. The method fuses two sources of information: a ranking model that scores documents (telling you which documents are most likely relevant) and a random sample of truly judged documents (giving you an unbiased ground truth signal). The ranking model acts as an informed prior: if it assigns high scores to many documents, you'd expect high recall; a small sample refines this belief. The model-assisted estimator corrects ranker bias by combining its calibrated scores with design-based sampling weights from classical statistics. This works because the two sources have complementary strengths: the ranker has no sampling error but may be biased; the sample has no model bias but high sampling variance. Combining them statistically reduces both errors. Conservative lower bounds then guarantee stopping rules won't overestimate and miss relevant documents.

Retrieving knowledge for language models from static graph communities misses dynamic query intent—asking about 'novel treatments' needs different subgraph slices than 'historical patterns'. This method works by searching for attributed communities (dense regions where nodes share both connectivity and semantic properties) on the fly. It finds self-complementary subgraphs: clusters of highly connected nodes with semantic overlap that answer the specific question. Why this works: real knowledge bases cluster semantically related facts together (papers on cancer treatment clump together), and communities capture both aspects—the connectivity ensures information is densely available, the shared attributes ensure relevance. High-order structures (beyond immediate neighbors) let the search jump between related clusters efficiently. Multi-granularity indexing reduces computation by pre-slicing the graph, so extracting relevant chunks is fast without sacrificing coverage.

Pricing data fairly requires matching supply and demand while accounting for data's unique property: it can be sold to multiple buyers simultaneously (non-rival). Classical competitive equilibrium determines prices where supply equals demand for rivalrous goods; adapting it to data means allowing simultaneous allocation to many buyers while clearing the market. The method works by modeling buyers' utility as improving with data quality (more data or better data makes predictions more accurate), so prices emerge where buyers stop wanting to buy because further data adds diminishing value. The existence proof shows equilibrium always emerges—a price vector exists where each buyer gets as much data as it wants at that price and all data finds willing buyers. Why this works: data utility has diminishing marginal returns (the tenth data point helps less than the first), so demand curves slope downward naturally. Price adjustment algorithms then find equilibrium by raising prices when data is scarce and lowering them when demand slackens.

Deepfakes span two independent sources of variation: semantic content (what the video shows—a person, a scene) and forgery technique (how it was faked—swapping faces, puppeting expressions). Traditional detection treats all fakes as one class and generalizes poorly because it conflates these two subspaces. The method uses orthogonal decomposition to separate parameters: some learn semantic invariance (recognizing content correctly regardless of domain), others learn forgery signatures (detecting the technical artifacts). A mixture-of-experts selects which expert activates based on detected forgery type, so face-swap fakes use one set of detectors while expression-puppet fakes use another. This works because the two problems genuinely require different feature detectors: semantic generalization needs broad visual understanding, forgery detection needs specific technical fingerprints. Disentangling them prevents the model from averaging conflicting signal and losing precision.

WebAssembly modules in browsers run with a single flat memory space, so any pointer bug lets attackers read or write anything. Isolating memory regions prevents this by making each region (stack, heap, globals) live in a separate memory instance, so pointer arithmetic in one region can't cross into others. The method works by analyzing pointers statically (reading the code without running it) to understand which regions each instruction accesses, then rewriting instructions to route memory access through the correct instance. This works because pointer analysis can prove, before execution, which memory regions are reachable from which code paths—so isolation is provably sound. Using the standard multi-memory feature adds no runtime overhead to access checking; isolation is architectural (enforced by the processor model itself). The 3% slowdown comes only from necessary instance-switching operations, not from added guards.

Predicting 12-volt battery load for vehicle power management is hard because driver behavior looks random, yet recent history carries signal: if the heater ran heavily in the last minute, it's likely still on. The method models this by computing conditional probability: given the observation that load was high recently, what's the distribution of load now? This works because electrical devices have inertia—heaters cool slowly, compressors don't switch instantaneously—so past state constrains present state probabilistically. Using 60 seconds of history as context reduces prediction uncertainty by 41% because that window spans the timescale at which load transitions happen. A learned model then maps historical context to precise load predictions. Why it works: conditional probability is mathematically sound because the recent past is informative—it screens off more distant history via the Markov property, so conditioning on recent observation gives the best available predictive power.

Detecting illicit accounts by behavior sequence is hard because fraudsters mimic normal users (adding friends looks innocent) and the same action in different contexts has different meanings. The method extracts category-specific patterns: recurring sequences typical of illicit users (rapid friend-adds followed by money requests) versus benign users (gradual friend-adds with conversation). It then encodes each action's context—what actions preceded and followed it in that sequence—so the model learns that add-friend followed by immediate transaction requests signals fraud, while add-friend in a slow conversational flow doesn't. This works because human behavior organizes into meaningful sequences: normal users follow social norms (conversation before transaction), fraudsters skip steps (immediate request). Context-aware encoding captures these sequential regularities. Combining extracted patterns with learned context ensures the model catches both obvious fraud patterns and subtle deviations that look innocent in isolation but reveal intent in sequence.
